toc.title: Why would you go into flight after fight?
How to move up from fight

blocks.p: What is the flight and fight state for, and how do you climb out of it? A listener sent me a question about this, and I want to use it to get some clarity on welcoming and discharging your own flight and fight energy. I'll treat it generally. I don't know this person's life beyond what they wrote, so this isn't specific advice for them or for you.
Here's what they wrote:

q: How do you climb up from anger? So it seems like the highest I've ever gotten was the fight state with a dash of safety just recently, and it was amazing. It made me feel on top of the world. Because of all the fight energy, I kept trying new things, and I felt like I was the...  I did realize it wasn't a calm, warm, balanced state. Very aware that it was full of fight energy, but at the same time, a HUGE improvement compared to the shutdown and freeze I'm in most of the time. Now, something that happened in therapy made me lose that dash of safety, and all I was left with was the dark side of fight: anger, irritation, frustration, disgust. And from there on, I started falling back down.

blocks.p: I love that you get this: fight with safety is a different experience than fight without safety. You call it the dark side of fight. I wouldn't call it the dark side. It is what it is, and I'll come back to that. But I completely get what you're saying, and I think it's helpful to frame it that way. With safety active at the same time, fight does become something different.
They went on:

q: So that is where my question comes from. How do you move up from fight/anger instead of back down? And another question that comes with that: what is flight, really? I have never understood that state very well, so maybe I don't even really know where to go next before I can get to safe and social. I don't understand how you can want to run away after you've been in fight and how that is actually better than fighting. Because I'm in fight right now, flight sounds like a coward. It sounds like less good than fight instead of better. But going from fight straight to safe and social seems like an impossibly big step indeed. So maybe understanding flight better might give me the answer to the main question.

blocks.p: There's a lot in that message, so let's break it into pieces: what flight and fight are, why you'd go into flight after fight, how to move up from fight, and why I'd rather not call any of these states good or bad.

Flight and fight are rungs on the [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system). The ladder is a metaphor for how our autonomic nervous system evolved in our body. At the top is the safe and social state. In the middle are flight and fight. At the bottom is the shutdown state.

Flight and fight are the same state. They're both sympathetic, and they're both mobility. But they occur sequentially: it's flight, and then fight. If you can't be safe, you run away. If you can't run away, you fight, you use aggression. If you can't use aggression, you shut down entirely. You go down the ladder in that order.

So flight and fight are two behavioral sets of the same state, and both of them require mobilization. That's a lot different from shutdown, which is immobilization. The safe and social state doesn't necessarily require mobilization, but it can use it, and it can also use immobilization.

Both flight and fight have an adaptive, functional behavior for survival. If you can't be with someone who's safe, or in a safe context, the body accesses its sympathetic state for flight, to escape the situation. If you can't escape, the body uses its fight behaviors to become aggressive, to get the danger to back off and create space.

blocks.h: Why would you go into flight after fight?

blocks.p: Why would you run away at all, especially if you're in a fight state? How does running away make any sense?

This is where we have to get really specific and shed any romantic ideas about how awesome it is to fight instead of run away. We have to set those judgments aside for a moment. These polyvagal states are survival mechanisms, because that's what they are. These autonomic shifts happen to increase the chances of survival. That's it. There is no other value to it. Any judgments we have about what these states look like, or how we should or shouldn't do them, don't matter here. They're a biological imperative in order to survive.

As far as I know, all organisms move toward resources for survival, for reproduction, for connection, and move away from things that would be a hindrance to that. They move away from potential dangers. In flight in particular, the organism moves away from danger. And again, there's no value to this, and I want to stress that heavily. It is what it is.
Human beings tend to place value on it. That's what's happening in "flight sounds like a coward." We have these words and judgments in our brain about how tough or strong we should be.

A great white shark does not shame itself as it swims away from an orca. Killer whales can actually hunt great white sharks. If the shark has to evade that, it doesn't shame itself for not fighting back, or for escaping, or trying to escape. Humans do, though.

With Polyvagal Theory, we have the concept of story follows state: the thoughts in our brain follow the state of our autonomic nervous system. First we have our autonomic state, and then that influences the words in our brain, the flavor of our thoughts. If we're in a fight state, our thoughts are going to be more shaming, potentially blaming, aggressive. If we're in a shutdown state, our thoughts are going to be more hopeless, expressing low worth or low motivation. The story matches the state. So "flight is less good than fight" could very well be a fight story.
The question is a little more specific, though. When we go up the ladder from shutdown into fight and become aggressive, why would we then escape? What's the function of escape?

The point of fight is to get the danger to back off. We create space by actually getting closer to it, in a sense, and we use the upper body: punching, throwing, pushing. The point of fight is not to pummel the danger into the ground, stand over it, beat your chest and feel like you're dominating. That's probably more of a rage thing. As you come up the ladder, fight is about getting the danger to back off.

Here's an easy example. A lion attacks a gazelle, jumps on it and subdues it. The gazelle isn't dead. It's in shutdown: it's fainted, collapsed, immobilized. The lion is worn out from sprinting after it and doesn't have the energy to eat yet, so it lies next to the gazelle, guarding it and catching its breath. Then some hyenas come along and distract the lion, and the lion has to protect its kill.

That gives the gazelle an opportunity to come out of shutdown and use its fight state. A gazelle isn't going to throw punches, obviously. But it might push up off the ground with its legs, using its power and its muscles, or do something more physically aggressive to create a bit more space if it needs to. What it's not going to do is hang around and beat up the lion. It's going to use its legs to run away, get back to its gazelle buddies, reconnect, and be in a safe and social state.

It's similar with human beings. If we have to, or we can, we might come out of shutdown and use our fight energy to create space, and then run away. Or, going down the ladder: if we can't be safe and can't run away, we may drop down to fight and become more aggressive to get the danger to back off, so that we can then use our flight energy to escape to safety and, hopefully, get back to people we can reconnect with.

Hunting might be different. There might be more of a sense of conquering, or power, and you're not going to run away from something you just killed. But that's not this. This is self-defense. In self-defense, fight isn't about completely dominating the danger. It's about getting it to back off so that we can escape. That's the basic idea of how it evolved within us.

I find in therapy that as my clients climb their ladder out of shutdown into fight, we want it to feel like power. We want it to have that safety attached to it. We want it to feel like power and responsibility and motivation. And if we can do that, what may happen next is that the flight state flavors their system more.

Flight is about escape. If we don't use it as escape, we feel it as anxiety, or nervousness, or worrying. So I've found it helpful to use the imagination with my clients. There's the famous example of Peter Levine and his client Nancy, where I think he first tried out this idea of having her imagine a tiger chasing after her. Just through imagination, she was able to have a physiological reaction of escape and discharge some of the stuck traumatic state she was in. At least in that moment. I don't think that was the entirety of it.

blocks.h: How to move up from fight

blocks.p: If you're stuck in fight, it's not simply an issue of using the defensive impulses. That can happen after you're more anchored in safety.

Well, it kind of is and it kind of isn't. Ultimately, yes, it comes down to: can I listen to my bodily impulses and sensations, be with them mindfully, use them, and discharge that stuck energy? But if you're stuck, you're stuck for a reason. Your capacity to do that might be way, way less.

If that fight energy is stuck within you, or just lingering there, it's felt as anger or irritability. That's what the listener described: it's not power, it's anger. Once the safety state is active, the same energy is experienced as power, motivation, competence, confidence. But you have to have the safety state active along with it.

That's exactly what they described as the highest they'd ever gotten: "the fight state with a dash of safety... it was amazing. It made me feel on top of the world." That sounds like exactly what I see with my clients, and with all of us. When fight energy is active, all it takes is a little bit of the safety state, enough of it, to shift it into a powerful, motivated feeling. "I can do this." A feeling of moving forward toward a goal.

It doesn't have to be about repelling a literal, physical danger in front of you. It can be about meeting a goal you have your mind on: "I can do this. I got this. I feel confident, and I'm going to make some steps forward toward my goal." But the safety state has to be active.
So if you're stuck in fight, or flight, or even shutdown, the work goes like this:

ol: Build safety first. Build the capacity to feel and stay in the safety state, even when you're experiencing, talking about, and feeling your stuck defensive state, including fight. Building the safety state is extremely important and absolutely necessary for everything after it.
Mindfully experience the defensive state. From your safety state, mindfully experience the fight state, or whatever defensive state you're in.
Feel its sensations and impulses. If you can be with it mindfully, you may be able to experience the sensations and the impulses of that state.

Discharge it, or build tolerance to it. You may be able to use movement, your imagination, or even creativity to discharge at least a little of it, or to build a tolerance to that stuck defensive state, the trauma that lives within you.

blocks.p: The listener didn't ask about this, but I think it's really important for many of us. Using power is really important for creating healthier boundaries between yourself and others.

There may be people in your life you need more space from. You're not going to go punch them, I hope, or fight them off and subdue them. But laying out a healthy, solid, clear, powerful boundary might be exactly what's needed. To do that, you need to be able to access a sense of power, confidence, and motivation: to say where your line is, and to get the people in your life who need to back off to back off. I think that's something we can all relate to.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: The last thing I want to go into is the idea that flight is not as good as fight, which could obviously be a fight story. Ladder climbing is not good, it's not bad, it's not better, it's not worse. It is what it is. There's no inherent judgment or value we should be giving to these things.

I know we do. I do. We all do it. But when it comes down to it, it's simply biology. All of our polyvagal states and mixed states serve a function. These are responses hardwired into our DNA that helped one organism of a species survive and reproduce, and it got passed on from one generation to the next. It's not good. It's not bad. It's not better. It's not worse. It simply is.

So I want to encourage all of us to start to word things differently, or at least to catch it and challenge ourselves to reframe it. Instead of saying "I feel better," which we all do, maybe reframe it as "I feel a shift happening." And yes, maybe that shift feels better. I get it. But take a step back and try to remove that evaluation. "I feel a shift happening. I feel a sense of lightness. I feel an impulse to connect." That's more descriptive of a safety state than "I feel better."

Maybe I'm nitpicking, but I think it's an important distinction when it comes to being with your stuck defensive state mindfully and out of curiosity. When you say there's a shift happening, there's more curiosity and less evaluation, and you're able to actually describe the sensations.

Of course we can describe experiences as good or bad. Feeling pain is a bad experience. Climbing the ladder out of shutdown and having more of a sense of expansiveness, we'd call that a good experience. Sure. But without the evaluation, it's just an experience, and I think that's more helpful. It comes with more curiosity than simply labeling things good or bad.

When I meet with my clients, I obviously ask, "How you doing?" They say, "Good." And I ask, "What does that mean?" Or they say, "I had a bad week." What does that mean? How do you feel right now? "I feel bad." In what way? Help me understand what that bad feeling is like. And when a client really cannot name how they feel, sometimes I'll even ask, "Is it a good feeling or a bad feeling?" So there's a usefulness to that kind of thinking. Think of it as a tool to get to the next step, because whatever you're feeling is not good or bad in and of itself. It might get grouped into those categories, but it's just an experience: a biological shift happening that you can mindfully experience and attend to. It is what it is, and I get to witness it. I get to experience it, describe it, maybe let my mind create images around what it's like for me in my body.

All of this, even my nitpicking, is central to polyvagal ladder climbing. When you look at things mindfully rather than judgmentally, I think you stand a better chance of climbing your ladder. That means describing rather than explaining.

A lot of times people say, "I feel this thing in my chest, it's an oval," and they'll start to describe its color. Or, "I feel this emptiness in my gut." Describing is a lot different from explaining: "I feel this way because..." Explaining has its usefulness. But first, or maybe eventually, begin to describe what you're experiencing, what it's like for you in that moment, rather than explaining why it's there.

So instead of avoiding what we feel, I'd encourage us to be able to mindfully experience it and be with it, hopefully with curiosity, interest, and a sense of neutrality. Not good or bad. It is what it is, and you get to experience it. You get to witness it.
